description: Stop doing sleep wrong: random bedtimes, second suns and caffeine tails. Retest your sleep score, then train your recovery hormones instead with a fixed wake time and a night routine that funds your recomp.

scenes.narration: Last night again. | Hours slept. | Wake quality. | Score out of one hundred. | Now the week's average. | Seven nights, roughly. | Write both scores down. | One night is weather. | The week is climate. | The old way slept randomly. | Done right sleeps by design. | At the end | I tell you | the design, all of it. | Your hormones are listening.

scenes.label: THE SCORE DONE RIGHT DEFENDS
scenes.narration: The line is a weekly average of eighty or above, with the nights arriving on schedule. That last clause is the entire episode. The old way treats sleep as a duration to grab when life allows, at hours that wander across the clock. Done right treats it as a rhythm to defend, because your hormones are paid by the rhythm, not the total. A man sleeping seven hours at the same time nightly will out-recover a man sleeping eight and a half at random times, and his waist will show the difference within a season. Keep your two scores in view. We are going to rebuild your night as a designed system: a fixed wake time as the cornerstone, light and caffeine as managed inputs, and a last hour that behaves like a landing strip instead of a second day.
scenes.sub: random nights / regular nights / recovery by design

lines: by the clock, not the total.
beats.title: THE CLOCK RULE

scenes.narration: Training your recovery hormones instead of just sleeping more starts with the clock rule: your brain does not schedule deep sleep by counting hours, it schedules it by rhythm, releasing the big growth hormone pulse in the first deep cycles of a night that begins when your body expects it to begin. Wander the bedtime and the pulse arrives late, shallow or split. Fix the timetable and the same hours pay out at a higher rate, which is why regularity beats duration in every study that separates the two. The cornerstone is the wake time, because it is the end of the night you can actually control. Fix it, defend it on weekends within an hour, and the bedtime will migrate earlier on its own as genuine sleepiness starts arriving on schedule. You are not becoming rigid. You are giving a hormone system the one input it was designed around: a predictable day. One more rhythm fact, the one that sells the wake time better than any lecture. Your cortisol is supposed to spike in the first hour after waking, a healthy pulse that starts the day's engine, and it fires on schedule only when the wake time is stable. A wandering wake time smears that pulse across the morning, leaving you groggy at nine and wired at midnight, the exact inversion of the design. Fix the wake time and both ends of the day correct themselves.

beats.text: THE LANDING STRIP: YOUR LAST HOUR

scenes.narration: Done right builds the last hour like a landing strip. Lights dim, because melatonin takes its orders from darkness. The room cools, because your core temperature must fall for deep sleep to open its gate. The phone parks outside the bedroom or across it, because a second sun in your hand resets the whole approach. And the day's open loops get closed on paper, ten minutes, so the brain stops running them as background processes at two in the morning. None of this is wellness decoration. Each item removes a specific thief identified in the mistakes episode, and together they convert the last hour from a second day into an approach path. Pilots do not hope for good landings. They fly a procedure. Your night deserves the same professionalism as your training, because hormonally it is the senior partner of the two. And treat the bedroom like a cave with a dress code: cool, dark and boring. Every object in it should argue for sleep and nothing else. The men who sleep like professionals do not have better willpower at midnight. They have better rooms, set up at noon, by a version of themselves who was thinking clearly. Environment is just willpower that was spent in advance, once, instead of nightly.

The routine has a morning half that most sleep advice forgets. Bright light in the first hour of the day, ideally outside for ten minutes, is the strongest clock-setting signal your body knows, anchoring the rhythm that will make you sleepy at the right hour tonight. A man who wakes at a fixed time and walks into daylight has set his midnight before his breakfast. This is the deepest sense in which sleep is trained rather than taken: the night is built by the day, input by input, light, caffeine timing, training load, the evening landing. Your light frame benefits quietly here as everywhere: your days already contain walks and movement, so the morning light anchor can ride on the step habit you built episodes ago. Systems that stack are systems that survive, and done right is nothing but the season's habits finally introduced to each other.

The final piece of done right is spending by the score. Each morning's number is a budget statement: over eighty, the night funded you fully, so train hard and eat to build. Sixty to eighty, train normally and protect the coming night. Under sixty, the session becomes technique, mobility and steps, a signal priced for the budget you have, and the evening becomes an early landing instead of a punishment workout. This is autoregulation, the practice that separates professionals from enthusiastic amateurs in every physical field. It feels like softness and grades like wisdom, because the man who adjusts never stacks the injury or the burnout week that deletes a month. Your score stops being a grade you judge yourself by and becomes an instrument you steer by, which is what every number in this season was always supposed to be.
Settle with me. Three rounds, forty-five seconds of horse stance, breathing slower every round, thirty seconds of rest. Tonight, this stillness goes with you to bed. Go.

beats.text: FORCING HARD DAYS ON EMPTY NIGHTS

scenes.narration: Installation, in order. Tonight, set the wake time and write it where you will see it at the alarm. Tomorrow, morning light within the first hour, caffeine done by noon. This week, build the landing strip: dim, cool, phone parked, loops closed on paper. Score every morning and spend the day by the budget. The old way's habits to bury: sleeping in to catch up, which just re-jet-lags the clock you are trying to set. Forcing hard sessions on empty nights and calling the wreckage discipline. And treating the routine as a phase, when rhythm is a permanent operating system, not a challenge with an end date. Thirty days of this and your score stops being weather. It becomes climate you chose.

beats.text: THE WEEKLY AVERAGE IS THE VERDICT
NOT THE BEST NIGHT. THE AVERAGE.

scenes.label: THEN WE AVERAGE A MONTH OF NIGHTS
scenes.narration: So, your weekly average. Under sixty: your nights are running a deficit your days cannot out-train, and the wake time is the single highest-value fix in your whole program right now. Sixty to eighty: the design is half built, and the landing strip probably closes your gap. Over eighty on a regular clock: your recovery hormones are funded like a professional's, and your remaining story is load and patience. Put your weekly average in the comments. Just the number, not your best night. In thirty days we average a month of nights, and that figure will explain your waist, your strength and your mood in one line of arithmetic.
scenes.sub: deficit / half built / funded - the average decides
